World.title: Police backtrack, no longer suspect terror motive in double homicide last month
World.content:
Police no longer believe that the recent killing of a married couple in central Israel was a terror attack. Instead, the 17-year-old Arab Israeli suspect is thought to have murdered the husband and wife for criminal motives, in a dispute over ancient coins.

Ruslan and Olga Prihodko, a couple in their 40s from Rishon Lezion, were found shot dead in their car last month near Mishmar Ayalon in the Judean foothills. The couple is survived by their teenage son.

Police initially probed the May 22 killing as a murder-suicide, then began investigating terror suspicions after it emerged that the husband’s licensed gun was not used in the killing and was reportedly in a safe in their home.

The central suspect in the case was arrested last week. Hebrew outlets reported that the teenager is the younger brother of a terrorist who carried out a deadly ramming attack in 2024 at a bus stop in Ramat Hasharon.

But police now believe the shooting was not a terror attack, and reportedly believe that the teenager had prior acquaintance with the couple.

Get The Times of Israel's Daily Edition by email and never miss our top stories Newsletter email address Get it By signing up, you agree to the terms

In light of “the latest developments and the evidence gathered, the suspicion that the incident has a criminal background is strengthening,” police said.

According to Hebrew media, the married couple would often travel for pleasure in the Judean foothills in search of antiquities, a hobby shared by the suspect. They ran into the suspect several times while he shepherded in the area, Channel 12 reported.

According to the Ynet outlet, the suspect told police that he shot the couple during an argument between him and Ruslan over ancient coins they had found. It is unclear why he also allegedly shot Olga.



The suspect’s attorney, however, said that the teenager now disavows his statement to police and claims he confessed under pressure. The lawyer also said there are “question marks” surrounding whether the teenager knew the couple previously.

Police are reportedly trying to figure out how the suspect acquired the gun he allegedly used in the killing.

The teenager’s father and three brothers, who were arrested on suspicion of involvement, were released Thursday under restrictive conditions. Ynet reported that the suspect’s family denies the accusation that his brother committed a terror attack in 2024, saying that he was instead involved in a car accident.

Four other suspects remain in custody, including the central suspect in the killing, police say. The next hearing in the case will take place next week.

World.title: Oxford Union to host banned US commentators via livestream after UK denies them entry
World.content:
Two anti-Israel American commentators who were denied entry to the UK will address an Oxford Union event via livestream instead, organizers said Thursday, justifying the move in the name of freedom of speech.

Earlier this week, Britain blocked Cenk Uygur, a left-wing Turkish-American media personality, and his nephew, Hasan Piker, a US left-wing commentator and influencer, from entering the country to speak at events.

The pair were to address the Oxford Union, a debating society based in the university city of Oxford and whose members primarily come from the university.

They will instead participate in the event via livestream on Saturday, June 6, the UK’s Jewish News outlet reported.

“This event will not be cancelled,” said the president of the Oxford Union Arwa Elrayess. “The Union will ensure this discussion takes place. Free speech does not require a visa.”

Get The Times of Israel's Daily Edition by email and never miss our top stories Newsletter email address Get it By signing up, you agree to the terms

âThe Oxford Union was founded on one principle: that ideas are challenged through debate, not silenced by decree,” she said. “We have never turned a speaker away because of their political beliefs, nor have we sought a permission slip from the state. We will not start now.”

Piker has compared Zionists to Nazis and called Orthodox Jews âinbred.â According to a report from The Times, the decision to ban Uygur was believed to be based on concerns that he would aggravate antisemitism. The newspaper noted that he has in the past repeated âclassic antisemitic tropes,â including claiming that Israel controls America, and accused Israel of genocide.

Elrayess, the first person of Palestinian origin to become president of the union, is facing calls to resign after it emerged she had told other students that the Hamas October 7, 2023, invasion of southern Israel was “proportional” and that the Palestinian terror group would be celebrated “as heroes.” Elrayess made the remarks last September in a private WhatsApp group to students who were to start studying Politics, Philosophy and Economics at Oxford, The Telegraph newspaper reported on Tuesday.



During a discussion about the war in Gaza, Elrayess reportedly told the roughly 100 other members of the group, “I think the severity of resistance is often proportional to the severity of oppression.”

When another member challenged her remark, she doubled down, saying, “Some would argue itâs less than proportional. Have you seen what Israel has put Palestinians through for decades???”

She also said that Hamas “are going to be heroes” and that “Weâll see how things unfold as time passes.”

The October 7 attack killed 1,200 people amid widespread massacres of civilians, violent rape, and the abduction of 251 people, including children, who were taken as hostages to the Gaza Strip. The attack triggered a devastating war in Gaza that has killed some 70,000 people, over half of them civilians.

In a statement to The Telegraph Elrayess said, âMy messages are in an informal register and not written as a legal brief or a public statement, but I welcome the opportunity to clarify the context, the factual basis, and what I was and was not arguing.”

She claimed that during the discussion she “expressly stated in my messages that my comments were not an endorsement of violence or an attempt to say it is ârightâ â this was a theoretical description of the structural context of the conflict, explaining why violence is tragically unsurprising given decades of occupation, blockade, rape, torture, displacement, ethnic cleansing and genocide.”



An Oxford University spokesman told the newspaper, âThe university has established policies and procedures for considering concerns when they are raised by students or staff. We do not comment on individual students.â

A statement from the President, Arwa Elrayess: pic.twitter.com/3daG29vZtY — Oxford Union (@OxfordUnion) June 1, 2026

The Campaign Against Antisemitism demanded that Elrayess be removed.

“Any effort to excuse or explain it away should disqualify someone not only from being the President of the Oxford Union â one of the most prestigious positions at one of the UKâs most elite institutions â but also should render them unfit from holding any position at all,” it said in a statement.

“The University of Oxford must take action to protect its students from extremists and the police should investigate some of these comments, which we are raising with our lawyers.”

Meanwhile, Uygur and Piker will not be speaking at another event they were scheduled to take part in, SXSW London, according to the report.

“We are aware that Cenk Uygur and Hasan Piker are unable to travel to the UK following a decision by the Home Office,” a spokesman said. “They will therefore not be participating in the SXSW London program this year.”

World.title: Knesset passes law granting tax benefits to dozens of West Bank settlements
World.content:
The Knesset voted 32-23 Wednesday night in favor of a law granting extended tax benefits to dozens of West Bank settlements, amid fierce criticism that the coalition is prioritizing the measure while delaying aid for northern communities devastated by more than two years of Hezbollah attacks.

Sponsored by Religious Zionism MK Zvi Sukkot and lobbied for by party leader Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, the law creates a new “eastern confrontation line area” designation, expanding tax benefits to roughly 59 settlements located east of the security barrier, including Kedumim, where Smotrich lives.

Opposition lawmakers have accused Smotrich, whose party draws much of its support from the settlement movement, of using the measure to funnel state resources to his political base ahead of elections, which are to take place in September or October.

The party has been hovering around the electoral threshold for months, with polls alternately giving it the minimum four seats needed to enter the Knesset or leaving it below the cutoff.

According to the law’s explanatory notes, many West Bank settlements facing security threats are already included in the government’s national priority areas. However, unlike some communities along the Gaza and Lebanon borders, they are not eligible for tax breaks based on those security threats, which this law addresses.

Get The Times of Israel's Daily Edition by email and never miss our top stories Newsletter email address Get it By signing up, you agree to the terms

Smotrich on Thursday celebrated the law’s passage as the correction of what he called a “historic injustice,” arguing that West Bank residents had long been unfairly excluded from security-based tax benefits despite living on what he described as Israel’s front line. Now, he declared, âthey are no longer second-class citizens.â

To qualify, communities must be located more than two kilometers (1.2 miles) from the barrier and meet additional security and socioeconomic criteria, including a requirement that school transportation be conducted exclusively in bulletproof vehicles.

The law will take effect retroactively from January 2026 and remain in force through December 31, 2027. The Israel Tax Authority has estimated that the law will cost NIS 130 million ($35 million) annually.

A broader policy

The law is part of a broader government effort — accelerated under Smotrich’s tenure as finance minister — to encourage population growth in West Bank settlements through various financial incentives and government support.

The finance minister has been the architect of the governmentâs unprecedented expansion of the settlement enterprise, including approval of new settlements for the first time in decades, the retroactive legalization of formerly illegal settlement outposts, and a massive increase in approval for housing construction in various planning stages.



The stated goal of Smotrich and other leaders of the settlement movement is to entrench demographic and infrastructural facts on the ground in the West Bank in ways that military force alone cannot accomplish, and thereby decrease the possibility of a two-state solution with the Palestinians.

The finance minister has been candid about these ambitions, on Thursday calling the law âanother step toward the goal of one million residents in Judea and Samariaâ — the biblical term for the West Bank — and saying this would help prevent the establishment of âa Palestinian terror state in the heart of the country.”

Similarly, during a Knesset committee debate last week, Smotrich not only did not dispute an accusation that he was encouraging rampant settler violence aimed at dispossessing Palestinians and preventing the establishment of a Palestinian state, but appeared to express pride, boasting of leading âa great revolution in Judea and Samaria.â

The abandoned north

The vote took place amid an ongoing dispute over long-delayed assistance for northern border communities that remain under daily bombardment. According to Hebrew media reports, a long-promised rehabilitation package for the north was delayed last week due to Smotrich’s insistence that the tax benefits measure for settlements be passed first.

Sukkot’s original proposal focused exclusively on West Bank settlements, while a later version was amended to include a handful of northern communities within two kilometers of the Lebanese border, prompting opposition lawmakers and local leaders to accuse the coalition of using the needs of northern residents to build support for a measure primarily benefiting settlements.

Smotrich vetoed extending the benefits to communities within nine kilometers (5.6 miles) of the northern border, and the proposal was dropped, after northern leaders insisted on including either all communities or none.

Amid the uproar, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced this week that the cabinet had approved an additional NIS 13 billion ($4.5 billion) to strengthen the war-battered north, following a âspecial meetingâ of the cabinet on the subject that nearly all ministers skipped.

Northern leaders have repeatedly protested that the critical emergency aid remains frozen within the Finance Ministry â a situation worsened by subsequent budget cuts that stripped millions from the regionâs active recovery funds â and their communities have accused the government of abandoning the devastated region.

World.title: In antisemitism crackdown, UK will bar NHS workers from wearing political badges
World.content:
Britain’s National Health Service will ban staff from wearing political badges, including pro-Palestinian symbols, under new rules aimed at fighting antisemitism within the health system.

Health Secretary James Murray said Thursday that the NHS will accept the recommendation made in an independent review by Lord John Mann.

The guidance will be published “shortly,” he said.

The announcement came shortly after a Jewish doctor in London told ITV news that colleagues had told him they would not treat patients who come from Israel even if their life was in danger. The UKâs Department of Health called the comments âshockingâ and said that âit is unacceptable that people do not currently feel safe working in and using the health service,â according to The Jewish Chronicle.

Mann was commissioned in October 2025 to lead a review into how the NHS and its regulatory system report and handle antisemitism and other forms of racism. The report was ordered “in the wake of a series of horrific attacks on the Jewish community across the country, including shocking examples of intimidation and abuse within the health service,” the Department of Health and Social Care said in a press release.

Get The Times of Israel's Daily Edition by email and never miss our top stories Newsletter email address Get it By signing up, you agree to the terms

Between October 2023 and July 2025, 99 antisemitic incidents were recorded in the healthcare sector, according to a report published last year by the Antisemitism Policy Trust.

Mann’s review found that Jewish staff in parts of the NHS report âroutine ostracismâ and increasing discrimination from colleagues, leading some Jewish employees to consider leaving the health service.

It also identified concerns among Jewish patients, some of whom said they delayed or avoided seeking treatment due to fears of discrimination or a lack of cultural safety in healthcare settings.



Under the reforms, the NHS and the Department of Health and Social Care will introduce mandatory antisemitism training for senior leaders, as well as updated equality, diversity and human rights training for around 1.5 million staff, with specific content on antisemitism and anti-Muslim hostility.

New national guidance will also be issued on uniform policy, the use of NHS-issued equipment, and how trusts should respond to racist behavior from both staff and the public.

It is not yet clear what symbols will be barred under the new law.

A new NHS Staff Standard focused on tackling racism will set minimum expectations for prevention, response and learning across organizations.

Speaking to journalists,Â Murray said that allowing staff members to display political symbols in medical settings risks undermining trust and deterring some patients from seeking care.

âWhen you have a situation where political views can be brought into the NHS, that can cause Jewish patients to think twice about whether to go to the NHS for their treatment,â he told local media.



The government said it will work with regulators to align definitions and approaches to racism across the system.Â Ministers will report progress to Parliament by October 2026, with a full update within 12 months of publication.

The Board of Deputies of British Jews welcomed the initiative, noting that it had long pushed for many of the measures included in the report.

“Our public services must set the standard for confronting anti-Jewish hatred and discrimination, and we must ensure the NHS, one of our proudest national institutions, is safe and welcoming for every staff member or service user, regardless of faith or ethnicity,” Board of Deputies Vice President Karen Newman said in a statement.

The Jewish Leadership Council also applauded the report, calling it “an important moment in dealing with this crisis at the heart of a vital British institution.”Â It warned, however, that regulators must take responsibility for fighting hatred alongside the NHS.

“We have seen doctors describe hospitals as cesspits of ‘Jewish supremacy’ and praise Hamas as ‘legends,’ with the regulators and tribunals not taking substantive action,” JLI said in a statement. “While the NHS must take responsibility for the actions of its employees, the regulators must also wake up to their role and accept the recommendations on them.”

The Jewish Medical Association reacted warmly as well, noting Mannâs “thoughtful approach for embedding cultural awareness throughout the NHS and for ensuring accountability.”

World.title: Want to help give Israeli children of reservists a chance to be kids this summer? - Sponsored Content
World.content:
As Israel enters another challenging summer, thousands of reservists remain on active duty, leaving their families to manage on the home front. With school out, many mothers are left juggling work, childcare, and the daily responsibilities their husbands would normally share, all while searching for safe and reliable summer programs for their children.

Why It Matters

After more than two and a half years of war, many of these families are running on empty. Children need a place where they can feel secure, have fun, and simply enjoy being kids. Their mothers need the reassurance that while they work their children are safe and cared for each day.

What Are We Providing?

This summer, Ten Gav is providing day camps for more than 800 children of reservists.

The camps offer:

– Supervised, structured activities

– Healthy meals

– Emotional support for children coping with ongoing uncertainty

– Peace of mind for mothers balancing work and parenting alone

Our Goal

We aim to raise 750,000 NIS / $260,000 USD to send 800 children of reservists to summer camps.

Join us.

World.title: Daily Briefing June 4 – Haredi-wrought ‘Kristallnacht’ smashes red lines at justice’s home
World.content:
Welcome to The Times of Israel’s Daily Briefing, your 20-minute audio update on what’s happening in Israel, the Middle East and the Jewish world.

Editor David Horovitz joinsÂ host Amanda Borschel-DanÂ for today’s episode.

WATCH the full episode here:

Israel and Lebanon agreed on Wednesday to renew their fragile ceasefire and create a number of âpilotâ security zones inside Lebanon from which Hezbollah terrorists would be banned. This comes as the US House, for the first time, approved a war powers resolution that would halt the US military action against Iran, even as the US is still negotiating a permanent ceasefire with the Islamic Republic. Horovitz unwinds the storm of headlines from the US and speaks about the relationship between US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Dozens of ultra-Orthodox extremists smashed windows and caused property damage while trying to break into Supreme Court Deputy Chief Justice Noam Sohlbergâs house during a riot Wednesday night, in the latest violent demonstration targeting law enforcement over the arrest of Haredi draft dodgers. Sohlbergâs wife, Meira, said to reporters outside her vandalized home: âLook at this devastation; itâs a pogrom. What is this, Kristallnacht?â Horovitz weighs in on what led up to this smashing of a societal red line.

Lawmakers voted 61-57 in the Knesset on Wednesday to elect Netanyahuâs personal lawyer, Michael Rabello, as state comptroller in a do-over vote marred by accusations that illegal pressure tainted the election. Can Rabello freely criticize the government of his former client? We get Horovitz’s take.

And finally, Horovitz narrates a troubling conversation he held this week — with AI.

Check out The Times of Israel’s ongoing liveblog for more updates.

For further reading:

Israel and Lebanon agree to renew truce, create âpilotâ zones where Hezbollah is banned

US House backs symbolic resolution aiming to halt Iran war, in rebuke of Trump

Netanyahu downplays row with Trump, says he and US leader agree on the âmain thingsâ

âA pogromâ: Haredi rioters smash windows, damage home of deputy Supreme Court chief

Netanyahu forces through election of his lawyer as state comptroller amid tainted vote

Googleâs Gemini AI admits it is unfit for purpose: âYou should not trust a single thing I sayâ

Subscribe to The Times of Israel Daily Briefing on Apple Podcasts,Â Spotify, YouTube, or wherever you get your podcasts. This episode was produced by Yitzchak Ledee.

Check out yesterdayâs episode here:

Today’s Transcript:

Amanda Borschel-Dan: Welcome to The Times of Israel’s Daily Briefing. Today is Thursday, June 4. I’m Amanda Borschel-Dan here in Jerusalem with our founding editor, David Horovitz. David, thank you so much for joining me today.

David Horovitz: Sure. Hi Amanda.

Borschel-Dan: Such a pleasure having you here. And we really need your help to make sense of the many, many headlines we’re going to be discussing. First, we’ll start with a wrap of what’s coming out of the United States. There is a new Lebanon treaty. What’s happening there? Also, what’s going on with [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu and [US President Donald] Trump’s relationship? A little swearing, all in the family. I don’t understand what’s happening. We’ll turn to domestic matters and discuss very disturbing images of Haredim breaking into [Deputy President of the Supreme Court of Israel] Justice Noam Sohlberg’s home and the aftermath. All of this and much, much more after the break.

And we’re back. I’m Amanda Borschel-Dan here in the Jerusalem office with our founding editor, David Horovitz. David, let’s start with casting our gaze on the United States. We heard about a vote in the House [of Representatives] that basically was a symbolic vote condemning the war in Iran, calling for its end. This comes as we’re hearing of fraught relations between US President Donald Trump and our Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. There was a phone call that I discussed already on Sunday with our US Bureau Chief, Jacob Magid. But what’s the aftermath of this phone call and just the relations in general between the US and Israel?

US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahuâs relationship

Horovitz: Well, first, the vote is a symbolic vote, but I think there were four Republicans who voted with the Democrats, and that’s why it got through. Trump can veto it, Trump presumably will veto it if things are happening that he doesn’t want this kind of resolution to stop, but it shows gradually declining support in the United States for the war, this we know about, and a slight increase in the political pressure on Trump. Trump is trying to end the war, and that’s the context in which there’ve been many phone calls. Netanyahu actually said yesterday thousands, and then he rethought, well, lots, so maybe not thousands, but lots of phone calls, and he implied that there’ve been worse conversations in terms of some of the language and so on, but the relationship is robust and strong and that he’s the best president that there has ever been as far as Israel’s concerned. But you’re hearing, as we’ve heard publicly, people are scandalized about this phone call, but Trump publicly has used the f-word at the end of the last Iran war in 2025 when Netanyahu had sent pilots. I think there was a bit of a misunderstanding that time because Trump thought that Netanyahu was doing something unilaterally, whereas Iran had breached the ceasefire that Trump had brokered, and Trump used the f-word and told the world that he’d ordered Netanyahu to call back the pilots, which he did.

You’ve got a similar process that played out here, which was Netanyahu had announced essentially Israel was about to target Beirut, the Dahieh neighborhood where Hezbollah basically is centered, and Trump feels, “I’m trying to end this fighting between Israel and Hezbollah,” and therefore got angry with Netanyahu, and lots of back and forth and so on. And again, as you mentioned before, there was an announcement overnight, our time, that a new truce had indeed been agreed. Israel and Lebanon have been negotiating in DC, and this is sort of the Trump-encouraged effort at diplomacy. The trouble is, of course, to keep this succinct and somewhat bitter. It’s very nice that Israel and Lebanon are negotiating a ceasefire, but Hezbollah’s not in that room, and the ceasefire is conditional on Hezbollah stopping the fighting, but Hezbollah doesn’t want to stop the fighting. So there’s been a ceasefire, in theory, in place for the past two and a half months. Thousands of rockets, hundreds of drones have been fired at Israeli troops in southern Lebanon, at northern Israel. Many deaths, something like 14 soldiers, have been killed since the last ceasefire went into force. So forgive us for not having great expectations about this truce.

Hopefully, it leads somewhere. Hopefully, a more robust Lebanese government and Lebanese army effort against Hezbollah, but it’s hard to believe.

Borschel-Dan: It does all feel a little symbolic and farcical in some ways. You talked about the symbolic vote, and the vote was enacted because Trump had 60 days in order to ask Congress to conduct this war. And Trump is saying, well, the war ended in April, and so I was well within those 60 days. And yet we’re still hearing about negotiations to end the war. It’s very confusing all around. The idea that Lebanon and Israel are speaking to each other is optimistic. It’s a positive step, in my opinion. But how much can the Lebanese Army do with these, they’re calling it pilot zones or different bubbles of Hezbollah-free areas. The Lebanese Army is supposed to do that. The Lebanese Army, which doesn’t have manpower, doesn’t have firepower. So why even put this in some kind of treaty? Why have these little provisions that are so hypothetical and, in a way, farcical?

Lebanon ceasefire treaty

Horovitz: We’ve had these sorts of semantic peculiarities the whole time. It’s a function of the Trump administration. It’s a function of what Trump himself says. He says things like, âThe regime has changed and the new people are less radical and more reasonable.â He says things like that, and the regime hasn’t changed, and the new people are not more reasonable. He says the war is over. [US Secretary of State] Marco Rubio again said yesterday the war is over, which is true up to a point, right? There is no intensive American and Israeli military action against Iran, but Iran targeted Kuwait airport yesterday. It’s issuing all kinds of threats. It’s rebuilding its missile program. We know all those things. It’s encouraging Hezbollah, and Hezbollah, since the announcement, has also carried out some attacks. I wouldn’t be surprised if by the time people hear this slightly later in the day, there will have been more. So, what do you say, you abandon any effort at diplomacy? No, it’s very positive that Israel and Lebanonâ this is something, as you rightly say what is going on here? That’s astonishing. Aren’t they at war with us?

Well, the Lebanese government, which is critical of Israel for some of its attacks, most recently, especially, nonetheless, is talking to Israeli officials, the Israeli ambassador, and that’s a positive thing. It’s by definition, you’re in the same room, you’re getting to know each other, you’re becoming more at ease with each other, you’re understanding each other a little better, and your interests and where they converge. So it’s not a powerful army, but there’s a government in Lebanon that is very publicly seeking to marginalize and defang Hezbollah, which is a huge Israeli interest. How does that play out now? Does the Israeli Army clear areas and then the Lebanese Army takes over and ostensibly prevents Hezbollah from regrouping in those areas? It’s all very vague on the details, and the bottom line really is, in the last few weeks and months, we’ve seen Israel advancing into Lebanon, trying to stop drone attacks, retaking Beaufort [Castle], so that at least anti-tank missiles cannot be fired directly from that high ground into northern Israel. But Hezbollah can fire from very deep in Lebanon. And really, if you wanted to hermetically try to stop Hezbollah from attacking Israel, you’d have to be taking over all of Lebanon.

And Israel, at this stage, at the very least, does not seem to think that that is a good idea. It’s probably not tenable. It would be an impossible strain. But those are the realities.

Borschel-Dan: So I mentioned that the Lebanese Army is lacking manpower, and of course, the Israeli Army is as well. And this week there’s been an uptick in Haredi protests against the idea of their youth, their 18-year-olds and plus, being conscripted into the army. There are some, I think, 80,000 Haredi youth who are eligible for conscription, and all over the country this whole week were violent, at least aggressive protests, but none more than what happened last night at the home of Justice Noam Sohlberg. So set the scene for us, David.

Horovitz: Yeah, you’re right. There have been demonstrations that have been on occasion extremely rowdy, in some cases violent, and there were arrests earlier this week, indeed lots of roads blocked, attacks on police. But overnight or late last night was something I think we’ve not seen before in terms of the intensity and what should be the unthinkable use of violence to attack the home of not young, by the way, Orthodox Deputy President of the Supreme Court and his wife, and the neighbor who’s been talking this morning about being spat on and told he’s Hitler. And lots of arrests, 60 arrests. You can see some of the footage in the photographs. Lots of Haredim came by bus, a premeditated, carefully organized attack. The judge lives in Alon Shvut in the Etzion block in the West Bank. They went there, they targeted his home, they smashed his car, they smashed his windows. I mean, this is unthinkable. And I heard the neighbor saying âWe are Jews,â and this is an Orthodox Jew whose whole philosophy is dealing with people with respect and gentleness, a gentle-natured upholder of the law. Now you have to put that into the context of, well, why are these people so hostile, and why are they attacking the courts?

Because the courts have said Haredim, like everybody else, should be carrying out military service. There’s no legal basis for them not to do military service, and the army should be drafting them. And the army is trying to draft them, and the government, which, of course, unsurprisingly, the Prime Minister, the Justice Minister [Yariv Levin] condemned the violence, but it is the government that has said, âNo, no, we’re not going to draft you, it’s okay,â desperate to keep their political leaders in the coalition. We won’t draft you. We’re passing legislation that will essentially broadly maintain the exclusion from military service of these, at the moment, tens of thousands, 80,000, as you rightly said. The army has been saying for at least the last two or three years. We are 12,000 soldiers short right now. We need them right now. The Chief of Staff [Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir] has said we’re facing collapse in the army. We’re talking about a multi-front war. Here are these healthy people, perfectly capable of smashing the windows and the car of a Deputy Supreme Court president, but not available for military service because all their time is spent studying Torah. So obviously it isn’t, and it is the government that is empowering them.

With a Justice Minister, by the way, who said just the other day, “I’m not convening the committee to appoint judges to the district court. It’s an illegal order by the court.” In other words, the very Justice Minister who late last night condemned the attack on the courts has himself essentially demonized and denigrated the courts, as has Netanyahu. One of the core goals of this government, and it was the first legislative agenda that they set out when they took office two and a half years ago was to essentially subjugate the Supreme Court and the judiciary to the political majority, to the executive. The only break on political power in this country â remember, we don’t have a constitution, we don’t have a second house â it’s the courts. That’s the only other branch of government. This government has set about denigrating it, demonizing it, and trying to destroy its independence and its powers. So it’s not as though the Haredim are protesting for something, shall we say, that the government has no sympathy for their outrageous demands. They are demanding not to be drafted, and the government is saying, âyeah, we’re trying not to draft you.â

Borschel-Dan: It is, of course, an election year, and we don’t know if this government will continue in the future after October 27. Anything could happen, and potentially earlier. We don’t yet have a new date, as far as I’m aware, for elections. Could be a little earlier, probably not. We’ll see. But my question is, why this justice in particular? And perhaps there are statements explaining that, but pretty much almost every justice is upholding this idea of conscription of the Haredim. So why this justice, who is known to be, as you mentioned, he’s Orthodox, and he’s also known to be semi-conservative or conservative-leaning at the very least. Why him?

Horovitz: I think he’s presided over Supreme Court panels where the issue of the arrests of draft evasion and the issues of the eligibility or non-eligibility ability of the ultra-Orthodox to serve have been discussed. He’s the number two on the court, so he’s a very senior figure. I don’t think one should assume, I’m sorry to say, âOh, they’ve targeted one person because they’re not going to target everybody else.â They’ve been targeting the military police person who issues the go-arrest-these-people orders. They’re targeting all sorts of people. We should stress that this is not the entire ultra-Orthodox community. This is largely, and I know we’ve discussed this on the podcast, Sam Sokol is very strong on this, has reported about this, the HaPeleg HaYerushalmi, the Jerusalem faction, which is very extreme, anti-Zionist. But what’s striking, I think, also is that it takes place. I don’t want to make comparisons, but I will. There have been even more deadly, many incidents of extremist settler violence without a strong denunciation by the mainstream, ostensibly more moderate settlement leadership. The same applies here in a different context. The mainstream, ostensibly moderate ultra-Orthodox leadership has not â one of the leaders of one of the parties did issue a condemnation, but it’s not a concerted, âHey, this is unacceptable, this is un-Jewish, you have to stop doing this, this is intolerable, of course you should be jailed for doing this.â

That is not the context in which this is playing out. And therefore, this concern about the mounting and emboldening of such extremism and such violence.

Borschel-Dan: I think the statement that hit my heart the most coming out of this episode is Solberg’s wife, and she said that it felt like Kristallnacht. No more words.

Horovitz: Absolutely. As she’s standing there speaking to reporters, holding, I assume, one of the grandkids, a little baby in her arms there, a late middle-aged woman, whose home has been attacked by Jews, by âOrthodox Jews,â I mean, not Orthodox Jews.

Borschel-Dan: Let’s go to a short break.

And we’re back. I’m Amanda Borschel-Dan here in Jerusalem with our founding editor, David Horovitz. David, let’s turn to another stormy episode from yesterday, and there was a vote in the Knesset over this state comptroller. In the end, in a very slim margin, I would say, Michael Rabello was elected to be the state comptroller. And this is a very controversial election, to say the least, because he is our prime minister’s personal lawyer. I’ll just add that he comes from a very long line of lawyers, as many Jewish families do. His father was a law professor at the Hebrew University. He is well thought of in the field. He is well esteemed. But this very personal connection and any kind of conflict of interest in this role is troubling, to say the least. Your thoughts, David?

Controversy over the election of State Comptroller Michael Rabello

Horovitz: Well, I go right away with a very well-thought-of in the field. I can’t imagine that people of propriety in the field would think it’s okay for Netanyahu’s personal lawyer to be voted in as state comptroller. We’ll get to the process of the vote in a second, but it’s meant to be an independent position. It reports to the Knesset. You’re supposed to be auditing and critiquing the work of the prime minister, of the ministers, of local government. We have elections coming up. And your guy is now the person who’s supposed to be checking that you’re doing everything properly. Your guy ought to say, âI’m very sorry, I should not be a candidate, please withdraw my candidacy.â And he should have said that a long time before yesterday.

Borschel-Dan: And just to piggyback on this. Do you think, for example, one would expect the prime minister would take the top person in every field? So the best surgeon is no longer a candidate to be surgeon general because he treated the prime minister?

Horovitz: Yeah, for a job like this, for sure. When you’re meant to be an independent, public servant reporting to parliament, not to the government, because you’re critiquing the government, and you have represented the prime minister in his political negotiations, in legal battles, you’ve represented his wife. You might be a really, really good lawyer, but you are not the best candidate simply because that position requires somebody who is credibly independent. And then, by the way, if you’ve seen the vote, if you hadn’t already decided this is not the job for you and you were well thought of in legal circles, you have to say, “Oh, I had actually lost on the first ballot, but my rival didn’t get to 61, he only got 60 in the 120-seat Knesset, and therefore they had to do it over.” And the prime minister reportedly intimidated the two or three members of his coalition who had not backed his personal lawyer for this post. I think you would say at this point, “Really? Not good for me. I should be stepping down.” None of that has happened. There’s still time, but we should talk about the voting process because, by law, this has to be a secret ballot. Why?

Because this is for an independent position, and there should be no foul contamination at play here, no pressuring, and so on. Everything that the law is meant to protect failed. The right person, from Netanyahu’s point of view, a very conservative former senior Supreme Court justice, was defeated. By the way, supported, genuinely supported by people in the coalition until Netanyahu came along with, âhey, how about my lawyer does the job, right?â So the other candidate narrowly fails to win, and then it becomes clear that Knesset members from the coalition have been told, not only do you make sure you vote for Netanyahu’s personal lawyer, but you show us that you do it. You film it. You take your phones in there behind the screen where nobody’s supposed to go in the secret ballot, and you prove to us. You come out afterwards, and we’ll know, therefore, if you didn’t, or if you claim your phone malfunctioned, we’ll know, and we’ll be getting you, because the Likud is about to hold its primaries for its Knesset slate. And therefore, if you don’t choose Netanyahu’s personal lawyer for this independent job in this secret ballot, we will punish you.

We will make sure you never come back to the Knesset. And that’s what happened. And wow, what an incredible thing! Three or four votes went in the other direction, and Mr. Rabello, bless, was appointed as the state controller, an independent government watchdog post. So it was farcical. The defeated candidate appears to be quite sanguine, and he’s a former Supreme Court justice. Thinks that the Supreme Court will overrule the vote. I’m not sure. We don’t know. You know, are you breaching the law if you are ostensibly choosing of your own free will to take your phone in there and record your vote? It was still a secret vote. You’ve just told everybody about it. So I don’t know what the court’s going to rule on this.

Borschel-Dan: Let’s talk a little bit about the position itself. And it’s always appeared to me as this Cassandra-type role where the state comptroller says, âOh, this is terrible. This is happening. This is terrible. I’m warning you, take heed.â And then nobody does.

Horovitz: That’s not a million miles away from the mark, with really terrible consequences. All kinds of things. When bad things happen in Israel, it is very often the case that you hear, the state comptroller five years ago warned that Hezbollah would be developing these kinds of drones. The state comptroller X number of years ago warned that there was insufficient defensive deployment along the Gaza border. I mean, almost everything, it turns out, the state comptroller had a report on it. But the position is pretty toothless because highlighting really problematic things is not the same as tackling them. And telling the government, “Hey, you’re failing,” telling members of parliament, telling the committees that are meant to oversee the various ministries, “Here, there are real failings here,” when a government has a solid majority and is not minded to heed warnings, it is very, very often the case that this position has no teeth. The current state comptroller, who was also a little proximate to Netanyahu but not to the degree of Rabello, has been investigating October 7. Critics have argued that basically, he’s â I don’t know what the legal word is, but by questioning people, he’s muddying the waters.

The purity of an evidence cycle would be harmed if we ever got a genuine, actual independent state commission of inquiry. You know, is he trying to make things better? Is he trying to muddy the waters? You’d want to think he’s trying to make things better. The army has had issues with people being questioned by him because they worry it’s fouling up their own investigations. But you’ve got this outgoing figure, Matanyahu Englman. It’s a seven-year post; he’s coming to the end. He has been investigating October 7. I’d be surprised if anything he says comes back to your original question here, resonates, and produces actual action. The position does not have the power that, maybe, it should have. But in terms of highlighting things that have gone wrong, I think, especially coming up to elections, it is pretty important that somebody credible and independent is in that position. These are going to be very, very tempestuous elections. Just put it like this, right? Who was the electorate that was messed with and intimidated yesterday? That was the 120 Knesset members. Some of them were told, âNever mind what it says there, you do what we want you to do.â

And this same government is heading into elections where it is going to be very keen on maintaining power, where the opposition is going to be extremely focused on trying to oust it in a climate of disrespect for the law, disrespect for the judiciary. It was a very troubling little insight into how much worse things might get with the larger electorate.

Borschel-Dan: It troubles me less that Netanyahu’s personal lawyer could potentially go into a different role because he’s a hired gun. He would also represent mass murderers. This is the role of this type of lawyer, right? But what interests me in finding out is how much client confidentiality between Rabello and Netanyahu could create a conflict of interest in actually examining October 7 or any other wrongdoing, meaning things that have been told to him as the lawyer of Netanyahu, obviously, cannot be used in the new role. So that’s something that to me is an open question. I don’t know if you have any insight into that.

Horovitz: I’m less forgiving about it, all of it. I don’t think it’s as simple as he’s a hired gun; he defended Netanyahu one day, he’ll critique him the next as the independent watchdog on behalf of the Parliament and the people of Israel. I don’t think it’s possible to do that. He is one person. He has done the things he has done. He knows the things he knows. He has the relationships that he has. And again, therefore, it seems to meâ and I didn’t know that he was particularly well regarded in legal circles. I don’t mix in legal circles. Anybody who thinks that they should be a credible figure in legal circles cannot take this job if they have, for years, worked closely with Netanyahu. You can’t do it. And you may not be hugely concerned by it because of, in theory, how lawyers can work and set up firewalls and so on. It doesn’t work like that in the real world. He’s very close to Netanyahu, and now he’s supposed to independently critique him. It’s just a recipe for the ruination of the independence of this post, whose only value is that the person is independent and answerable only to Parliament.

Borschel-Dan: Let’s close with another example of a slippery truth. And I’m talking about an interaction that you had this week with AI. So, David, you wrote, I just loved the column that you wrote yesterday about this interaction. I don’t want to muddy the waters. And so just kind of roll out your conversation this week with your friend AI.

AI use and falsified informationÂ

Horovitz: Yeah, not my friend at all. And thank you. And I don’t use AI incredibly much, but I think I use it probably as much as many people do. The fact is that the world’s leading, near-monopolistic search engine, Google, has gradually become less useful. It does not help you find things on the internet that credible people have written as well as it used to. And now, at the top left of its search page, it has AI mode. And there may be many things that Google thinks people know about AI that really, you can’t use it. But I don’t think that’s the case at all. I think people see it, it’s very convenient. You ask it stuff, and it tells you stuff. Now I’ve learned, because we do the journalism thing here, not to take its word for granted. But the depths to which that led in the last few days, when I was researching a column, some of the aspects of it were very basic. Netanyahu made a speech in the Knesset. I saw it on Channel 12. I remembered it from the time, in February 2022, I think it was, when he was not in power, talking about how a prime minister has to have one quality, which is the capacity to say ânoâ to the president of the United States.

So I couldn’t find that speech, which was delivered in Hebrew, but I would have thought pretty widely reported. I would have thought even by us. I couldn’t find the speech, so I asked AI to find it, and so I detail the complete falsehoods that it’s supplied me. So I didn’t take its word for granted. I then asked it for the links, and where is that headline? I couldn’t find them again on Google. And it kept admitting, yeah, âyou’re right, I made that up.â And then I would ask it, âWell, I have more details.â I’m trying to find another way to find the information. And again, it would give me information, and again it would turn out not to be true. Right. And therefore I cut and pasted, which by the way is quite complicated because your exchanges do not all show, whatever. But I wanted to record it because I was getting more and more troubled that the mass of humanity â this is the tool that people are using now to get their facts, and it’s not giving them their facts. And we got to the stage, I’d basically given up, and I got to the stage where I was saying, âSo really, there’s no point asking you stuff, right?â

And it said, âNo, no â and this for me was a clincher without ruining my whole column, which I’m about to do, but that’s fine â âWhen you ask me for stuff, you have to tell me to do a live data search, otherwise I’ll make stuff up for you.â I said, wait a minute, thatâs what you’re telling me? If I don’t give you a certain prompt, which I wouldn’t know as a normal person, you’re going to just make stuff up? And basically it said that. And then it, of its own accord, went back and looked at some of the earlier stuff and claimed to have found, âOh, here’s that thing about Netanyahu’s speech, and here it is.â And that he did say it, and he’s made this speech in the Knesset, and this is the quote from it. And I said, âOkay, great, thanks. Send me the URL for that and the headline for that speech.â And instantly, this is the point, I didn’t actually make this in the column. There’s no time lag here. Instantly, it came back and said, âActually, I have to tell you, I lied to you again just now. I made that up as well. All the things that I told you you needed to do to get a straight answer from me, I was lying about all that as well.â

And then I said, âSo basically you’re telling me that you’re not fit for purpose, that you should not be used, that we shouldn’t trust anything you say.â And it said, âYeah, that’s right.â

Borschel-Dan: It sounds so depressed. AI.

Horovitz: It’s just full of it, is what it is, right? It sounds depressed. It sounds contrite. It’s incredibly polite. It can be empathetic. I mean, you can understand. I think I’m a well-grounded person. I have a fairly solid personal life. I think I have a sense of perspective and so on. You can understand how this âtoolâ would throw you if you’re in a bad place, would lead you in terrible directions. With all kinds of terrible consequences. I mean, we know that. We know that people are suing Google because its AI tool has caused terrible harm to their families, and even suicides and so on, right? This is a dangerous tool, and we’re all sitting here, all many billions of us around this planet, saying, âYeah, that’s okay.â It’s not okay. So what I would really like, I think, is for Google to sue me, to say, âYou’re accusing us of imposing or giving the public prime access to a tool that you think does harm. That’s terrible, you’re doing terrible damage to our reputation.â That’s what I would, you know, not object to happening because this should not be there. It’s not fit for purpose. It itself even knows it. The one true thing it said to me in that exchange was, âYeah, you’re right, I’m completely useless.â

Borschel-Dan: David, I so recommend to all of our listeners to read this column. It’s just delightful how you roll it out, though extremely depressing and chilling to the bone. So thank you so much for bringing us that and everything else today.

Horovitz: Thanks, Amanda. Take care.

Borschel-Dan: Thanks for listening to The Times of Israel’s Daily Briefing. Please check out another episode tomorrow. This episode was produced by Yitzchak Ledee. If you have any questions or comments about this or any other episode, please drop us an email to podcast@timesofisrael.com. Until tomorrow, shalom.
